title: Writing an LLM from scratch, part 21 -- perplexed by perplexity
summary: Raschka calls out perplexity in a sidebar, but I wanted to understand it in a little more depth.
markdown:
I'm continuing through chapter 5 of [Sebastian Raschka](https://sebastianraschka.com/)'s book "[Build a Large Language Model (from Scratch)](https://www.manning.com/books/build-a-large-language-model-from-scratch)", which covers training the LLM. [Last time](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/10/llm-from-scratch-20-starting-training-cross-entropy-loss) I wrote about cross entropy loss. Before moving on to the next section, I wanted to post about something that the book only covers briefly in a sidebar: perplexity.

[Back in May](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/05/llm-from-scratch-15-from-context-vectors-to-logits), I thought I had understood it:

> Just as I was finishing this off, I found myself thinking that logits were interesting because you could take some measure of how certain the LLM was about the next token from them. For example, if all of the logits were the same number, it would mean that the LLM has absolutely no idea what token might come back -- it's giving an equal chance to all of them. If all of them were zero apart from one, which was a positive number, then it would be 100% sure about what the next one was going to be. If you could represent that in a single number -- let's say, 0 means that it has only one candidate and 1 means that it hasn't even the slightest idea what is most likely -- then it would be an interesting measure of how certain the LLM was about its choice.
> 
> Turns out (unsurprisingly) that I'd re-invented something that's been around for a long time. That number is called perplexity, and I imagine that's why the largest AI-enabled web search engine borrowed that name.

I'd misunderstood. From the [post on cross entropy](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/10/llm-from-scratch-20-starting-training-cross-entropy-loss), you can see that the measure that I was talking about in May was something more like the simple Shannon entropy of the LLM's output probabilities. That's a useful number, but perplexity is something different.

Its actual calculation is really simple -- you just raise the base of the logarithms you were using in your cross entropy loss to the power of that loss. So if you were using the natural logarithm to work out your loss L, perplexity would be eL, if you were using the base-2 logarithm log2 then it would be 2L, and so on. PyTorch uses the natural logarithm, so you'd use the matching `torch.exp` function.

Raschka says that perplexity "measures how well the probability distribution predicted by the model matches the actual distribution of the words in the dataset", and that it "is often considered more interpretable than the raw \[cross entropy\] loss value because it signifies the effective vocabulary size about which the model is uncertain at each step."

This felt like something I would like to dig into a bit.

When we're training an LLM, the cross entropy loss we get after one step is based on a whole bunch of different sequences and their associated targets. A sequence like "The fat cat sat on the", with its target " fat cat sat on the mat", will have one prefix sequence for each token in the input sequence, and each one will map to one target token:

-   "The" -> " fat"
-   "The fat" -> " cat"

...and so on. And every other input sequence/target sequence in the batch will have the same.

Our cross entropy loss is the arithmetic mean of all of those per-sequence/target losses.

To unpick perplexity, I found it easiest to start thinking about what it meant on a per-sequence/target level -- as always, I'll use

```
"The fat cat sat on the" -> " mat"
```

Now, in the [last post](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/10/llm-from-scratch-20-starting-training-cross-entropy-loss), we found that the loss for this specific pair was this:

L\=−logpcorrect

...where pcorrect was the probability that the model assigned to " mat" -- that is, the correct answer -- in the distribution we got by softmaxing the logits. This is what the full cross entropy formula reduces to if the real distribution that we're comparing our model to is just a one-hot distribution with a probability of one for the target token, and zero for everything else.

Let's work out the perplexity for that; if we use the natural logarithm ln, then we need to raise it to the power of e, so we get this:

Perplexity\=e−lnpcorrect

I had to [refresh](https://www.mathcentre.ac.uk/resources/uploaded/mc-ty-logarithms-2009-1.pdf) my knowledge of logarithms a bit for this next bit, but we can simplify that. (Apologies for readers who are more current in this for the step-by-step derivation.)

To start: log1 in any base is 0, so we can rewrite the perplexity equation in a slightly more complex form as:

Perplexity\=eln1−lnpcorrect

There is an identity for all logarithms:

logxy\=logx−logy

So we can apply that rule and get:

Perplexity\=eln1pcorrect

By the definition of logarithms,

blogbx\=x

...so we can finally simplify to:

Perplexity\=1pcorrect

Phew. That exercised a few brain cells that had been sleeping since the early 90s. Let's think about what it means in some specific cases.

Firstly, imagine that the LLM is 100% certain that the next token is " mat". That means that the probability vector it has output (logits post-softmax) has a one in the position for " mat" (and therefore zeros everywhere else). That means that pcorrect\=1, so perplexity is 1/1\=1.

Now imagine that the LLM had no idea which token might come next. We'll assume that its output is a probability distribution where every number is 1/N, where N is the number of tokens in the vocabulary. That means that our perplexity is N.

This gives a hint as to what Raschka meant by "signifies the effective vocabulary size about which the model is uncertain at each step". In the first case, it was certain -- that is, the subset of the vocabulary that it was considering as options had a size of 1, and that's the number we have for perplexity. In the second case, it was considering all N tokens in the vocab as possibilities, so that's the number we have for perplexity.

We can extend that -- let's say that it was dithering between four out of the N tokens in the vocabulary of N, thinking they were all equally likely (and the others had zero probability). Each of those would have a probability of 1/4, and so perplexity would be 4.

Or would it? There is a wrinkle.

Remember, we're only considering the probability it assigns to the correct token -- our target for the training. Let's say that we have a four-token vocab, and the target in the training item we're considering is the second token (index 1 in the lists that follow).

We might get this probability distribution:

```
[0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25]
```

But we might also get this one:

```
[0.0, 0.25, 0.0, 0.75]
```

In both of those cases, pcorrect is 0.25, so our perplexity will be 4. But while in the first case we could reasonably say that it was uncertain about which option to pick from a vocab size of four, in the second case it's really only looking at a vocab size of two at the most -- indeed, a number between one and two would seem reasonable, probably closer to one.

The important thing, though, is that it was *wrong* about the choice it ascribed the high probability to in that second case. So I think we can refine the description a little. Perplexity doesn't measure how many vocab items the model was choosing between (which, again, would be something like the Shannon entropy of the probability distribution) -- that's an oversimplification of what Raschka was saying. It has to include some kind of reference to what the *right* answer is.

Let's go back to [something from the last post](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/10/llm-from-scratch-20-starting-training-cross-entropy-loss#certainty), the section on "Certainty". Our training for LLMs is slightly artificial, at least in the case of a single sequence-target pair. In our example where we're feeding in "The fat cat sat on the" and telling it that the target is " mat", we're using a one-hot vector for the target distribution -- that is, we're saying that the sequence *must* continue with " mat". That's obviously incorrect -- it could be any of a number of possible tokens, like " lap" or " dog" or " desk".

We don't do that kind of "label smoothing" training with LLMs, because it would be hard to set up and we're training on so much data that the different gradient updates average out to the real distribution over time. But imagine if we did. We have a probability distribution p which is the real distribution of the next tokens, and our LLM's prediction q, so cross-entropy loss (using natural logarithms) is:

H(p,q)\=−∑xp(x)·lnq(x)

So our perplexity is:

Perplexity\=exp(−∑xp(x)·lnq(x))

Pulling the negation back inside the sum we get:

Perplexity\=exp(∑xp(x)·(−lnq(x)))

Now we can apply that −lna\=ln1a rule we went through step-by-step above:

Perplexity\=exp(∑xp(x)·ln1q(x))

Now another high-school rule; if you take something -- say, z -- to the power of a+b+c -- that is, za+b+c -- it's the same as multiplying za, zb and zc. For example:

101+2+3\=101×102×103\=10×100×1000\=1000000\=106

I don't remember seeing it at school, but there is a big-pi operator for doing the product of a series to match the familiar big-sigma for sum, so we can express that (for the exp operator that we're using to mean e to the power of something) as:

exp(∑ixi)\=∏iexp(xi)

So we can apply that to our perplexity equation to get this:

Perplexity\=∏xexp(p(x)·ln1q(x))

Yet one more high-school rule:

za·b\=(za)b

So let's swap around our terms in the exp function:

Perplexity\=∏xexp(ln1q(x)·p(x))

...then apply that:

Perplexity\=∏x(exp(ln1q(x)))p(x)

Now, clearly exp(lnx)\=x, so we can simplify:

Perplexity\=∏x(1q(x))p(x)

I hope you found that as fun as I did :-)

Now, the 1/q(x) that we have there is the equivalent of the perplexity measure that we were using for our original one-hot calculation -- the inverse of the probability that the model assigned to a given token. What we're doing is iterating over all of the predictions, working out that number, and taking it to the power of the real-world probability of it happening. Those results are then multiplied together to get our overall perplexity.

Let's think of how that works with real numbers.

Imagine that a token doesn't exist at all as an option in the real-world probability distribution p. That means that p(x) will be zero, so the contribution it makes to the overall perplexity will be its per-token perplexity to the power of zero, which is one -- as we're multiplying numbers together, that means that it will have no effect.

If it is 0.5 in the real-world data, then the contribution of the perplexity will be scaled down by being square-rooted (that is, raised to the power of 1/2).

And if it is 1 in the real-world data, it will be raised to the power of 1 -- that is, it will be fed through unchanged.

So we've got a setup where we're taking the per-token perplexity and we're using the real-world probabilities to scale how much it contributes -- the more likely a token is in the real world, the higher the power we're raising it to (though these powers are all less than one, being probabilities, so each item will contribute less than its per-token perplexity).

And, of course, if we feed in a one-hot vector for p then all of the terms but one will have p(x) of zero, so they’ll be raised to the power 0 (i.e. 1). Then for that case where p(x) is one, it will be passed through unchanged -- that is, it will collapse to the original equation:

Perplexity\=1qcorrect

OK, so at this point we've shown that perplexity, if used against a cross entropy loss that compares how the LLM is doing with respect to the real world probabilities, will give us a number that combines how "confused" the model was about each possible output token, scaled by the probability of that token in the real world. It's not actually all that different from cross entropy loss (which is unsurprising, given that it's just a number raised to the power of that loss).

How does that help in our world where we're using one-hot vectors?

Let's start by bringing back in something we put aside at the start of this post. For a given training run, we have a batch of sequences, with targets for each prefix sequence. So for that run we have b·n sequence/target pairs for a batch size of b and a sequence length of n. Let's call that number T.

The cross entropy loss we have for the ith of those pairs, using our one-hot equation, is:

Li\=−lnq(tcorrect)

Now, we're just taking the arithmetic mean of those different per-pair losses to work out the cross entropy of the whole training batch. Let's write that as:

L\=1T∑t\=1T−lnq(tcorrect)

Now we work out the perplexity:

Perplexity\=exp(1T∑t\=1T−lnq(tcorrect))

Using −loga\=log1a again, we get:

Perplexity\=exp(1T∑t\=1Tln1q(tcorrect))

Moving the division inside the sum:

Perplexity\=exp(∑t\=1T1Tln1q(tcorrect))

Back to high school maths:

a·logx\=logxa

So we can go to:

Perplexity\=exp(∑t\=1Tln(1q(tcorrect))1T)

Using the rule we used above for converting the exponential of a sum to the product of exponentials:

Perplexity\=∏t\=1Texp(ln(1q(tcorrect))1T)

...and then using our blogbx\=x rule, we get:

Perplexity\=∏t\=1T(1q(tcorrect))1T

Now, we could refactor that one step further, like this:

Perplexity\=(∏t\=1T1q(tcorrect))1T

...which shows that the combined perplexity over all sequence/target pairs is the geometric average over all of the per-token perplexities (just as with an arithmetic average of n numbers, you add them all and then divide by n, for the geometric average you multiply all of your numbers and then take the nth root). And that's interesting, but let's take another look at the first version:

Perplexity\=∏t\=1T(1q(tcorrect))1T

...and then compare it to the formula we had for perplexity where we're using the full cross entropy, comparing our LLM's output to a probability distribution p that captured the real distribution of next tokens:

Perplexity\=∏x(1q(x))p(x)

They're tantalisingly close! But those exponents are the difference -- in the first one, we have a constant 1/T exponent, but in the second we have p(x)

Now let's imagine that we have done our training run on a really large and diverse dataset, so large and diverse that the distribution of targets matches what language as a whole has, and we want to work out the perplexity over that big dataset.

As a toy example with essentially the same properties, let's say that all of our training sequences are "the fat cat sat on the", and that in reality that sequence is completed by " mat" 60% of the time, " lap" 30% of the time, and " dog" 10% of the time. Conveniently enough, we have ten training sequences, six of which have " mat" as the target, three have " lap", and one has " dog".

Once again, our perplexity formula is this:

Perplexity\=∏t\=1T(1q(tcorrect))1T

...and what that means is that we have this bit:

(1q(tcorrect))1T

...multiplied ten times, one for each of our sequence/target pairs. Six of those times will be for the " mat" case, so we can just multiply those together (and substitute 10 in for T, as we know that that is what it is):

(1q(mat))610

We can do the same for the " lap" and " dog" cases too, so the whole formula reduces to:

(1q(mat))610×(1q(lap))310×(1q(dog))110

Those exponents look familiar! We said up-front that the real world distribution (which our dataset matched) was " mat" 60% of the time, " lap" 30% of the time, and " dog" 10% of the time.

The equation is the product of the per-token perplexities, taken to the power of their respective probabilities, and that is:

Perplexity\=∏x(1q(x))p(x)

What we've shown is that using the one-hot probability distribution for the targets doesn't actually break anything; perplexity is always calculated relative to the actual diversity of the possible next tokens in the dataset that we've provided.

So when we average perplexity across a large enough dataset, we're effectively estimating the same number we'd get if we compared the model directly against the true probabilities of the language itself.

### Conclusion

I hope that was an interesting read -- for me, at least, it was a valuable reminder of some basic maths from long ago.

And if there's one thing to take away from this, I think it's this:

Perplexity is, like loss, a metric you use on a model against a particular dataset (aka *corpus*). It measures how many correct tokens the model was choosing between for each prediction it made, weighted by how likely each one is. In practice, you often see benchmarks saying things like:

> Our model achieved a perplexity of 15.2 on our validation set, and 18.5 on WikiText-103.

What that means is that it was effectively choosing between about 15.2 plausible next tokens on the validation set, and 18.5 on WikiText -- presumably the latter differed from the training data more than the former.

And finally, while you might intuitively think that our use of one-hot probability distributions would cause problems with the maths, for a well-balanced (which in practice just means "large and diverse") corpus, it all balances out because the more common a particular next token choice is in the dataset, the more times it will contribute perplexity to the total, and it will all balance out.

That's all for now! For the next post, let's see if I can wrap up training :-)

[Here's a link to the next post in this series](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/10/llm-from-scratch-22-finally-training-our-llm).

We'll assume that its output is a probability distribution where every number is 1/N, where N is the number of tokens in the vocabulary. That means that our perplexity is N. 现在想象 LLM 完全不知道接下来是什么词元。假设它输出的概率分布中每个数字都是 1/N，N 是词表中词元的数量。那么困惑度就是 N。 This gives a hint as to what Raschka meant by "signifies the effective vocabulary size about which the model is uncertain at each step". In the first case, it was certain -- that is, the subset of the vocabulary that it was considering as options had a size of 1, and that's the number we have for perplexity. In the second case, it was considering all N tokens in the vocab as possibilities, so that's the number we have for perplexity. 这解释了 Raschka 所说的“表示模型在每一步不确定的有效词表大小”。第一种情况中，模型确定了——它考虑的词表子集大小是 1，困惑度正是 1。第二种情况中，它把词表中的全部 N 个词元都视为可能，因此困惑度是 N。 We can extend that -- let's say that it was dithering between four out of the N tokens in the vocabulary of N, thinking they were all equally likely (and the others had zero probability). Each of those would have a probability of 1/4, and so perplexity would be 4. 还可以推广：假设它在词表 N 中的四个词元之间犹豫，认为它们概率相等（其他词元概率为零）。每个概率为 1/4，所以困惑度为 4。 Or would it? There is a wrinkle. 真的是这样吗？这里有个细节。 Remember, we're only considering the probability it assigns to the correct token -- our target for the training. Let's say that we have a four-token vocab, and the target in the training item we're considering is the second token (index 1 in the lists that follow). 记住，我们只考虑模型分配给正确词元（训练目标）的概率。假设词表有四个词元，而当前训练项的目标是第二个词元（下面列表中的索引 1）。 We might get this probability distribution: 我们可能得到这样的概率分布： ``` [0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25] ``` But we might also get this one: 但也可能得到这样的分布： ``` [0.0, 0.25, 0.0, 0.75] ``` In both of those cases, pcorrect is 0.25, so our perplexity will be 4. But while in the first case we could reasonably say that it was uncertain about which option to pick from a vocab size of four, in the second case it's really only looking at a vocab size of two at the most -- indeed, a number between one and two would seem reasonable, probably closer to one. 两种情况下 pcorrect 都是 0.25，所以困惑度都是 4。但第一种情况下，可以合理地说模型在四个词元组成的词表中不确定选哪个；第二种情况下，它最多只在两个词元之间选择——实际上，介于 1 和 2 之间的数字似乎更合理，而且可能更接近 1。 The important thing, though, is that it was *wrong* about the choice it ascribed the high probability to in that second case. So I think we can refine the description a little. Perplexity doesn't measure how many vocab items the model was choosing between (which, again, would be something like the Shannon entropy of the probability distribution) -- that's an oversimplification of what Raschka was saying. It has to include some kind of reference to what the *right* answer is. 不过重要的是：第二种情况下，模型把高概率分配给了错误的词元。所以我认为可以稍微改进描述。困惑度并不衡量模型在多少个词表项之间选择（那更像概率分布的 Shannon 熵）；这是对 Raschka 说法的过度简化。它必须以某种方式参考*正确*答案。 Let's go back to [something from the last post](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/10/llm-from-scratch-20-starting-training-cross-entropy-loss#certainty), the section on "Certainty". Our training for LLMs is slightly artificial, at least in the case of a single sequence-target pair. In our example where we're feeding in "The fat cat sat on the" and telling it that the target is " mat", we're using a one-hot vector for the target distribution -- that is, we're saying that the sequence *must* continue with " mat". That's obviously incorrect -- it could be any of a number of possible tokens, like " lap" or " dog" or " desk". 回到[上一篇文章](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/10/llm-from-scratch-20-starting-training-cross-entropy-loss#certainty)的“确定性”一节。至少对于单个序列—目标对，LLM 训练有点人为。在输入 “The fat cat sat on the”、告诉模型目标是 “ mat” 的例子中，我们对目标分布使用独热向量——也就是说，我们声称序列*必须*以 “ mat” 继续。这显然不正确——它也可能是 “ lap”“ dog”“ desk”等许多词元。 We don't do that kind of "label smoothing" training with LLMs, because it would be hard to set up and we're training on so much data that the different gradient updates average out to the real distribution over time. But imagine if we did. We have a probability distribution p which is the real distribution of the next tokens, and our LLM's prediction q, so cross-entropy loss (using natural logarithms) is: 我们不对 LLM 做这种“标签平滑”训练，因为设置困难，而且训练数据足够多，不同梯度更新会随着时间推移平均成真实分布。但假设我们这么做。设概率分布 p 是下一个词元的真实分布，LLM 的预测为 q，那么（使用自然对数的）交叉熵损失是： H(p,q)\=−∑xp(x)·lnq(x) So our perplexity is: 因此困惑度是： Perplexity\=exp(−∑xp(x)·lnq(x)) Pulling the negation back inside the sum we get: 把负号移入求和内部，得到： Perplexity\=exp(∑xp(x)·(−lnq(x))) Now we can apply that −lna\=ln1a rule we went through step-by-step above: 现在应用上面逐步推导过的 −lna=ln1a 规则： Perplexity\=exp(∑xp(x)·ln1q(x)) Now another high-school rule; if you take something -- say, z -- to the power of a+b+c -- that is, za+b+c -- it's the same as multiplying za, zb and zc. For example: 再用一个高中数学规则：把某个数（例如 z）提升到 a+b+c 次方，即 za+b+c，等于把 za、zb 和 zc 相乘。例如： 101+2+3\=101×102×103\=10×100×1000\=1000000\=106 I don't remember seeing it at school, but there is a big-pi operator for doing the product of a series to match the familiar big-sigma for sum, so we can express that (for the exp operator that we're using to mean e to the power of something) as: 我不记得在学校学过，但确实有一个大 Π 运算符，用来表示一串数的乘积，与熟悉的表示求和的大 Σ 对应。因此（对我们用来表示 e 的幂的 exp 运算符）可以写成： exp(∑ixi)\=∏iexp(xi) So we can apply that to our perplexity equation to get this: 所以可将它应用到困惑度方程： Perplexity\=∏xexp(p(x)·ln1q(x)) Yet one more high-school rule: 再来一个高中数学规则： za·b\=(za)b So let's swap around our terms in the exp function: 因此交换 exp 函数中的项： Perplexity\=∏xexp(ln1q(x)·p(x)) ...then apply that: ……然后应用该规则： Perplexity\=∏x(exp(ln1q(x)))p(x) Now, clearly exp(lnx)\=x, so we can simplify: 现在显然 exp(lnx)=x，所以可以化简： Perplexity\=∏x(1q(x))p(x) I hope you found that as fun as I did :-) 希望你和我一样觉得这个推导很有趣 :-) Now, the 1/q(x) that we have there is the equivalent of the perplexity measure that we were using for our original one-hot calculation -- the inverse of the probability that the model assigned to a given token. What we're doing is iterating over all of the predictions, working out that number, and taking it to the power of the real-world probability of it happening. Those results are then multiplied together to get our overall perplexity. 这里的 1/q(x)，等价于原始独热计算中使用的困惑度指标——模型给某个词元分配的概率的倒数。我们遍历所有预测，计算这个数，并将其提升到该词元在现实中出现的概率次方。然后把这些结果相乘，得到总体困惑度。 Let's think of how that works with real numbers. 想想它如何处理真实数字。 Imagine that a token doesn't exist at all as an option in the real-world probability distribution p. That means that p(x) will be zero, so the contribution it makes to the overall perplexity will be its per-token perplexity to the power of zero, which is one -- as we're multiplying numbers together, that means that it will have no effect. 假设某个词元根本不是现实概率分布 p 中的选项。这意味着 p(x)=0，它对总体困惑度的贡献就是该词元困惑度的 0 次方，即 1——由于我们在相乘，它不会产生影响。 If it is 0.5 in the real-world data, then the contribution of the perplexity will be scaled down by being square-rooted (that is, raised to the power of 1/2). 如果它在真实数据中的概率是 0.5，那么困惑度的贡献会通过开平方（即提升到 1/2 次方）而缩小。 And if it is 1 in the real-world data, it will be raised to the power of 1 -- that is, it will be fed through unchanged. 如果它在真实数据中的概率是 1，就提升到 1 次方——也就是原样传递。 So we've got a setup where we're taking the per-token perplexity and we're using the real-world probabilities to scale how much it contributes -- the more likely a token is in the real world, the higher the power we're raising it to (though these powers are all less than one, being probabilities, so each item will contribute less than its per-token perplexity). 因此，我们用现实概率缩放每个词元困惑度对整体的贡献：词元在现实中越可能，提升它的幂越高（不过这些幂都是小于一的概率，所以每项贡献都会小于其单词元困惑度）。 And, of course, if we feed in a one-hot vector for p then all of the terms but one will have p(x) of zero, so they’ll be raised to the power 0 (i.e. 1). Then for that case where p(x) is one, it will be passed through unchanged -- that is, it will collapse to the original equation: 当然，如果 p 是独热向量，除了一个项外所有项的 p(x) 都是零，所以它们提升到 0 次方（即 1）。p(x)=1 的那一项则原样传递——也就是说，化简回原始方程： Perplexity\=1qcorrect OK, so at this point we've shown that perplexity, if used against a cross entropy loss that compares how the LLM is doing with respect to the real world probabilities, will give us a number that combines how "confused" the model was about each possible output token, scaled by the probability of that token in the real world. It's not actually all that different from cross entropy loss (which is unsurprising, given that it's just a number raised to the power of that loss). 好了，到这里我们已经证明：如果把困惑度应用于比较 LLM 与真实世界概率的交叉熵损失，它会把模型对每个可能输出词元有多“困惑”结合起来，并按该词元在现实中的概率加权。它其实与交叉熵损失并没有太大不同（并不意外，因为它只是损失的幂）。 How does that help in our world where we're using one-hot vectors? 这对我们使用独热向量的情况有什么帮助？ Let's start by bringing back in something we put aside at the start of this post. For a given training run, we have a batch of sequences, with targets for each prefix sequence. So for that run we have b·n sequence/target pairs for a batch size of b and a sequence length of n. Let's call that number T. 先把文章开头暂时放下的一点带回来。一次训练运行有一批序列，每个前缀序列都有目标。因此，批次大小为 b、序列长度为 n 时，共有 b·n 个序列/目标对。把这个数量记为 T。 The cross entropy loss we have for the ith of those pairs, using our one-hot equation, is: 用独热公式，第 i 个序列/目标对的交叉熵损失是： Li\=−lnq(tcorrect) Now, we're just taking the arithmetic mean of those different per-pair losses to work out the cross entropy of the whole training batch. Let's write that as: 现在我们取这些逐对损失的算术平均值，计算整个训练批次的交叉熵。写成： L\=1T∑t\=1T−lnq(tcorrect) Now we work out the perplexity: 现在计算困惑度： Perplexity\=exp(1T∑t\=1T−lnq(tcorrect)) Using −loga\=log1a again, we get: 再次使用 −loga=log1a： Perplexity\=exp(1T∑t\=1Tln1q(tcorrect)) Moving the division inside the sum: 把除法移入求和： Perplexity\=exp(∑t\=1T1Tln1q(tcorrect)) Back to high school maths: 回到高中数学： a·logx\=logxa So we can go to: 因此可以得到： Perplexity\=exp(∑t\=1Tln(1q(tcorrect))1T) Using the rule we used above for converting the exponential of a sum to the product of exponentials: 使用上面将“和的指数”转换为“指数的乘积”的规则： Perplexity\=∏t\=1Texp(ln(1q(tcorrect))1T) ...and then using our blogbx\=x rule, we get: ……然后使用 blogbx=x 规则，得到： Perplexity\=∏t\=1T(1q(tcorrect))1T Now, we could refactor that one step further, like this: 我们还可以再向前整理一步： Perplexity\=(∏t\=1T1q(tcorrect))1T ...which shows that the combined perplexity over all sequence/target pairs is the geometric average over all of the per-token perplexities (just as with an arithmetic average of n numbers, you add them all and then divide by n, for the geometric average you multiply all of your numbers and then take the nth root). And that's interesting, but let's take another look at the first version: 这说明，所有序列/目标对合在一起的困惑度，是所有词元困惑度的几何平均（算术平均 n 个数是相加后除以 n；几何平均则是相乘后取 n 次方根）。这很有意思，不过再看看第一个版本： Perplexity\=∏t\=1T(1q(tcorrect))1T ...and then compare it to the formula we had for perplexity where we're using the full cross entropy, comparing our LLM's output to a probability distribution p that captured the real distribution of next tokens: 然后与使用完整交叉熵时的困惑度公式比较：完整交叉熵将 LLM 输出与捕捉下一个词元真实分布的概率分布 p 进行比较： Perplexity\=∏x(1q(x))p(x) They're tantalisingly close! But those exponents are the difference -- in the first one, we have a constant 1/T exponent, but in the second we have p(x) 两者非常接近！差别在于指数：第一个使用常数 1/T，第二个使用 p(x)。 Now let's imagine that we have done our training run on a really large and diverse dataset, so large and diverse that the distribution of targets matches what language as a whole has, and we want to work out the perplexity over that big dataset. 现在假设训练运行使用了一个非常庞大且多样的数据集，大到目标分布与整个语言的分布相匹配；我们想计算这个大数据集上的困惑度。 As a toy example with essentially the same properties, let's say that all of our training sequences are "the fat cat sat on the", and that in reality that sequence is completed by " mat" 60% of the time, " lap" 30% of the time, and " dog" 10% of the time. Conveniently enough, we have ten training sequences, six of which have " mat" as the target, three have " lap", and one has " dog". 举个具有相同本质的玩具例子：假设所有训练序列都是 “the fat cat sat on the”，现实中该序列有 60% 的概率以 “ mat” 完成，30% 以 “ lap” 完成，10% 以 “ dog” 完成。方便的是，我们有十个训练序列，其中六个目标是 “ mat”，三个是 “ lap”，一个是 “ dog”。 Once again, our perplexity formula is this: 再一次，困惑度公式是： Perplexity\=∏t\=1T(1q(tcorrect))1T ...and what that means is that we have this bit: 这意味着有下面这一项： (1q(tcorrect))1T ...multiplied ten times, one for each of our sequence/target pairs. Six of those times will be for the " mat" case, so we can just multiply those together (and substitute 10 in for T, as we know that that is what it is): ……对每个序列/目标对重复相乘十次。其中六次是 “ mat” 情况，因此可以将它们先相乘（并将 T 替换成 10，因为我们知道它就是 10）： (1q(mat))610 We can do the same for the " lap" and " dog" cases too, so the whole formula reduces to: “ lap” 和 “ dog” 情况同样处理，于是整个公式化简为： (1q(mat))610×(1q(lap))310×(1q(dog))110 Those exponents look familiar! We said up-front that the real world distribution (which our dataset matched) was " mat" 60% of the time, " lap" 30% of the time, and " dog" 10% of the time. 这些指数看起来很熟悉！我们一开始说过，现实世界分布（数据集与之匹配）是 60% 的 “ mat”、30% 的 “ lap” 和 10% 的 “ dog”。 The equation is the product of the per-token perplexities, taken to the power of their respective probabilities, and that is: 方程就是把每个词元困惑度提升到其对应概率的幂后相乘，也就是： Perplexity\=∏x(1q(x))p(x) What we've shown is that using the one-hot probability distribution for the targets doesn't actually break anything; perplexity is always calculated relative to the actual diversity of the possible next tokens in the dataset that we've provided. 我们已经证明：用独热概率分布表示目标并不会破坏任何东西；困惑度始终是相对于所提供数据集中可能下一个词元的实际多样性计算的。 So when we average perplexity across a large enough dataset, we're effectively estimating the same number we'd get if we compared the model directly against the true probabilities of the language itself. 因此，在足够大的数据集上平均困惑度，实际上是在估计这样一个数：如果直接将模型与语言本身的真实概率比较，我们也会得到这个数。 ### Conclusion 结论 I hope that was an interesting read -- for me, at least, it was a valuable reminder of some basic maths from long ago. 希望这篇文章读起来有趣——至少对我来说，它让人重新想起很久以前学过的基础数学，很有价值。 And if there's one thing to take away from this, I think it's this: 如果要记住一件事，我认为就是： Perplexity is, like loss, a metric you use on a model against a particular dataset (aka *corpus*). It measures how many correct tokens the model was choosing between for each prediction it made, weighted by how likely each one is. In practice, you often see benchmarks saying things like: 困惑度和损失一样，是针对特定数据集（也叫*语料库*）评估模型的指标。它衡量模型每次预测时，在多少个正确词元之间进行选择，并按每个词元的可能性加权。实际中，你常会看到基准测试这样写： > Our model achieved a perplexity of 15.2 on our validation set, and 18.5 on WikiText-103. 我们的模型在验证集上的困惑度为 15.2，在 WikiText-103 上为 18.5。 What that means is that it was effectively choosing between about 15.2 plausible next tokens on the validation set, and 18.5 on WikiText -- presumably the latter differed from the training data more than the former. 这意味着，在验证集上模型实际上大约在 15.2 个合理的下一个词元之间选择，在 WikiText 上约为 18.5 个——可能后者与训练数据的差异比前者更大。 And finally, while you might intuitively think that our use of one-hot probability distributions would cause problems with the maths, for a well-balanced (which in practice just means "large and diverse") corpus, it all balances out because the more common a particular next token choice is in the dataset, the more times it will contribute perplexity to the total, and it will all balance out. 最后，虽然直觉上你可能认为使用独热概率分布会给数学带来问题，但对于平衡良好（实践中就是“规模大且多样”）的语料库，一切会相互抵消：某个下一个词元选择在数据集中越常见，它对总困惑度的贡献次数就越多，最终会平衡起来。 That's all for now! For the next post, let's see if I can wrap up training :-) 暂时就到这里！下一篇文章，看看我能否把训练部分收尾 :-) [Here's a link to the next post in this series](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/10/llm-from-scratch-22-finally-training-our-llm). [这是本系列下一篇文章的链接](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/10/llm-from-scratch-22-finally-training-our-llm)。
titleZh: 从零开始构建 LLM（第 21 篇）——困惑于困惑度
summaryZh: Raschka 在侧栏提到了困惑度，但我想更深入地理解它。
